claims.text: Cyclic mechanical disruption and partial reformation of a protective passivating oxide film governs the coupled tribocorrosion response of high-entropy alloys.
Wear-induced rupture of the passivating film accelerates localized corrosion.
The alloy initially has an intact passivating oxide film.
Oxide-film integrity and reformation ability are the structural mediators of degradation.
Sliding wear mechanically disrupts the protective oxide layer.
Disruption of the oxide layer exposes fresh, unpassivated metal to the corrosive environment.
The oxide film can partially reform under static conditions.
Cyclic rupture prevents full stabilization of the oxide film.
Prevention of full film stabilization accelerates localized corrosion and overall degradation.
Relative to static corrosion or lower-wear conditions, cyclic mechanical wear will produce moderately greater wear depth.
Relative to static corrosion or lower-wear conditions, cyclic mechanical wear will produce a significantly higher localized-corrosion rate.
The increases in wear and localized corrosion will enhance total degradation.
The prediction applies when wear intermittently disrupts the film without completely removing it or preventing its formation.
The mechanism may not operate at extremely low wear because the passivating film remains intact.
The mechanism may not operate during continuous high-energy wear because oxide-film reformation becomes impossible.
The quantitative relationship between film-rupture frequency and localized-corrosion rate may depend on alloy composition and environmental conditions.
